\chapter{Asking a Yes-or-No Question}
\label{ch:mr-polar-question}
\hlchaptermodality{33}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can turn any statement I own into a yes-or-no question with kaa, hear one carried by the voice alone, and write it with one trailing mark.}

Complete MR-R33-ask-and-answer and run a two-turn exchange: ask whether there is tea and answer it, then ask permission and decline.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[… kā?]{… \mr{का}? (… kā?) — the yes-or-no question}

\label{lesson:MR-C33-kaa-polar}



\begin{quote}
Retrieve the last two items by name: the tag \textbf{\mr{ना}}, and the sentence-final \textbf{\mr{नाही}}. Both go at the end. So does this one.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \mr{का} at the end}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{माहीत} \mr{आहे} \mr{का}?} — \emph{māhīt āhe kā?} — \textbf{Do you know?}
\end{quote}

Marathi leaves the person out when it is obvious, so this three-word question needs no pronoun at all.

Take a statement, put \textbf{\mr{का}} on the end, and nothing else moves — no word order, no verb. Marathi does not turn a sentence around to ask; it appends.

\textbf{\mr{ना}} says \emph{this is so, agree with me}. \textbf{\mr{का}} says \emph{I do not know, tell me}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{चालेल} \mr{का}?} — \emph{chālel kā?} — \textbf{Is that all right?}
\end{quote}

That is how you ask permission, and the answer comes back as the \textbf{\mr{चालेल}} you already own.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
Speakers often drop \textbf{\mr{का}} and let pitch do the work: \textbf{\mr{चहा}?} with a rising voice is a complete offer. Say \textbf{\mr{चहा}.} flat, then \textbf{\mr{चहा}?} rising. A listening paper gives you the rise without the particle, so the ear must hold both.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{māhīt āhe kā?} and answer it — \emph{ho} or \emph{nāhī}
  \item \emph{chālel kā?} and answer it — \emph{chālel}
  \item \emph{chahā?} with the rise, and \emph{chahā.} flat
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\mr{का}} on the end do, and what else moves? (\textbf{Makes a yes-or-no question; nothing}.) How does it differ from a final \textbf{\mr{ना}}? (\textbf{\mr{ना} expects agreement; \mr{का} does not know the answer}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[praśnacihna · udgārcihna]{? and ! — the marks that go only at the end}

\label{lesson:MR-W33-question-mark}



\begin{quote}
You can now ask a yes-or-no question out loud. On paper, the rising voice is gone. Something has to take its place.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: one mark, and only at the end}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{चहा} \mr{आहे} \mr{का}?}
\end{quote}

Marathi writes the question mark exactly where English does: \textbf{one} mark, at the \textbf{end}, and nowhere else. If you have met Spanish, this is worth naming — Spanish opens a question with an upside-down mark as well as closing it, and Marathi does not. There is nothing at the front of the sentence to warn you.

That is the practical consequence: in a printed Marathi sentence the only signal that you are reading a question may be the last character on the line, or the little \textbf{\mr{का}} just before it. Read to the end before you decide.

And the rising voice you learned last lesson leaves no trace at all. Written down, \textbf{\mr{चहा}?} has to carry the mark, because there is no pitch on paper.

\subsection*{Script: the exclamation mark}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{नमस्कार}!}
\end{quote}

Same rule, same place, one mark. It marks a greeting or a raised voice, and it never doubles at the front either.

\subsection*{Writing — copy and mark}
Write \textbf{\mr{चहा} \mr{आहे} \mr{का}?} once. Then write \textbf{\mr{नमस्कार}!} once. Check that each line carries exactly one mark and that it is the last thing on the line.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many question marks does a written Marathi question carry, and where? (\textbf{One, at the end}.) So what must you do before deciding whether a printed sentence is a question? (\textbf{Read to the end of it}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[… kā? — ho / nāhī]{Ask it, then answer it}

\label{lesson:MR-R33-ask-and-answer}



\begin{quote}
A question in Marathi is a statement with \textbf{\mr{का}} on the end and one mark on the page. Say one, then write it — and write \textbf{\mr{नमस्कार}!} underneath, so the two end marks stand side by side.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chahā āhe kā?} — answer \emph{ho}
  \item \emph{māhīt āhe kā?} — answer \emph{malā māhīt nāhī}
  \item \emph{chālel kā?} — answer \emph{nako, dhanyavād}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the three answers a \textbf{\mr{का}} question can get. (\textbf{\mr{हो}}, \textbf{\mr{नाही}}, \textbf{\mr{नको}} — and the last only for an offer.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
